title: On 15 January 1919, a storage tank in Boston's North End collapsed and killed 21 people.
description:
On 15 January 1919, a storage tank in Boston's North End collapsed and killed 21 people. The tank held roughly 2.3 million US gallons of molasses, around 13,000 tons, and it gave way just after half past twelve in the afternoon.

The speed investigators estimated for the wave of molasses that tore through the neighbourhood, fast enough to lift a train carriage off its tracks.

It surged fast while warm, then thickened as it cooled, trapping people who might otherwise have escaped. Molasses is roughly 40 percent denser than water. A 2016 Harvard study modelled the flow, judged the reported speed credible, and found that the thickening molasses made rescue far harder.

Owner of the tank. A court appointed auditor spent three years hearing evidence before finding the company responsible and ordering close to 628,000 dollars in damages, one of the first class action settlements of its kind in Massachusetts.

For decades afterwards, people in the North End said you could still smell molasses there on a hot day.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Molasses_Flood - Read in full. Establishes the date and time (15 January 1919, around half past twelve), tank capacity (about 2.3 million US gallons, roughly 13,000 short tons), an estimated wave speed of 35 miles per hour, the toll of 21 dead and about 150 injured, the lawsuit against United States Industrial Alcohol Company that produced a roughly 628,000 dollar damages award after a court appointed auditor's multi year hearing, the enduring local claim that the neighbourhood smelled of molasses for decades afterwards, and the 2016 Harvard University study that modelled the flow and judged the reported speed and the resulting rescue difficulties to be credible.
